# **Project Overview**

Student food insecurity is now widespread in Australia, and campus pantries such as the University of Sydney FoodHub must ration limited food, volunteers and shelf space. Campus Pantry is a PostgreSQL database that replaces spreadsheets with one consistent record of who booked, who attended, who staffed each shift and what stock moved. Students book a 30-minute session and receive a QR token; staff check students in, roster supervisors and volunteers, and record purchases, batches and stock counts. A Python command-line prototype exercises every workflow, while triggers, constraints and row-level locks keep the data correct under concurrent use.

# **1\. Problem and Requirements**

## **1.1 Problem and Motivation**

Studies at Australian universities found that 48% of surveyed students were food insecure (Whatnall et al., 2020), and one repeated survey found the rate rose from 42% in 2022 to 53% in 2024 (Kent et al., 2025). The University of Sydney FoodHub gives students free groceries, but they must register before collecting during limited weekday hours (Students' Representative Council \[SRC\], n.d.). With limited space, stock and volunteers, access must be booked and rationed. Doing this in spreadsheets causes double bookings, overfull sessions, lost stock history and understaffed shifts. These are consistency problems across related data, which is what a DBMS with constraints and transactions is built to prevent.

## **1.2 Users and Stakeholders**

* **Students** – view free places, book one session per day, cancel, and present a QR token.  
* **Volunteers** – request shifts and see whether staff approved them. A person can be a student and a volunteer at the same time.  
* **Staff (supervisors and assistants)** – check students in, approve volunteers, record exceptions, purchases and stock counts.  
* **Pantry managers** – need demand, attendance, waste and low-stock reports to plan purchasing.

## **1.3 Data Requirements**

The system stores people identified by UniKey and their roles; shifts and their 30-minute sessions; bookings with status, QR token and any override details; staff duty assignments and volunteer requests; products, purchase records and lines; stock batches with unique StockNumbers and expiry dates; and an append-only history of physical stock counts, plus per-shift opening/closing quantities and receipt/waste adjustments.

## **1.4 Business Rules and Scope**

| ID | Rule |
| :---- | :---- |
| BR1 | A UniKey (4 lowercase letters \+ 4 digits) identifies each person; roles may overlap. |
| BR2 | A day has three 2-hour shifts, each containing four 30-minute sessions inside the shift's time range. |
| BR3 | A session holds at most 50 active (non-cancelled) bookings. |
| BR4 | A student has at most one active booking per date, unless a named staff member records an override with a reason. |
| BR5 | Each booking has a unique QR token; ATTENDED requires an attendance time; a token can be checked in once. |
| BR6 | Students may arrive late; unscanned bookings become ABSENT only after the 16:00 close. |
| BR7 | A shift can be OPEN or CLOSED only with exactly one MAIN\_SUPERVISOR and one ASSISTANT; no person is rostered on overlapping shifts. |
| BR8 | Each received batch gets a StockNumber (STK-\#\#\#\#\#\#) and must trace to a purchase line for the same product. |
| BR9 | Stock counts are never overwritten; quantities are non-negative. |

**Out of scope:** real SSO login, email delivery of QR codes, food weights, and multi-site pantries.

## **1.5 Representative User Operations**

* A student sees how many places remain in each session today and books one.  
* Front-desk staff scan a QR token and mark the student attended.  
* After closing (16:00), staff mark all remaining bookings as no-shows.  
* A supervisor approves a volunteer's shift request and views the day's roster.  
* Staff record a closing count and see each shift's opening, received, wasted, closing and dispensed quantities.  
* Managers list products below their reorder threshold, batches near expiry, and sessions at 80%+ capacity.

# **2\. Conceptual Design (ER Model)**

## **2.1 Final ER Diagram**

![][image1]

**Figure 1\. Final ER diagram of Campus Pantry in lecture notation (arrow \= key constraint, thick line \= total participation, triangle \= IsA, double ellipse \= multivalued attribute, double rectangle / double diamond \= weak entity / identifying relationship).**

## **2.2 Entities and Attributes**

| Entity | Identifier | Important attributes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Person (superclass) | UniKey | full\_name, email, contact |
| Student / Volunteer / Staff (subclasses) | UniKey (inherited) | degree\_level, student\_category / is\_active / staff\_code, is\_active |
| Shift | shift\_id | shift\_date, start\_time, end\_time, status (PLANNED/OPEN/CLOSED) |
| Session | session\_id | session\_date, start\_time, end\_time, capacity |
| Booking | booking\_id | status, qr\_token, created\_at, attendance\_at, admin\_override, override\_reason |
| Product | product\_id | product\_code, product\_name, category, counting\_unit, low\_stock\_threshold |
| PurchaseRecord | purchase\_id | purchase\_date, reference, notes |
| PurchaseLine | purchase\_line\_id | quantity, unit\_cost |
| StockBatch | stock\_number | batch\_code, received\_on, expires\_on, received\_qty |
| StockCount | stock\_count\_id | counted\_at, count\_type (OPENING/CLOSING/SPOT\_CHECK), counted\_qty, notes |
| ShiftRequest (weak entity) | UniKey of its Volunteer \+ shift\_id of its Shift (no discriminator) | status (PENDING/APPROVED/REJECTED), request\_date, reviewed\_at |

staff\_code, qr\_token and product\_code are also unique, but ER notation shows only one key per entity, so they are declared as candidate keys in the logical schema (Section 3.1).

Booking is modelled as an entity rather than a relationship between Student and Session because it has its own lifecycle (CONFIRMED → ATTENDED / ABSENT / CANCELLED), its own identifier (the QR token) and its own optional relationship to the staff member who approved an exception. A student can also book the same session again after cancelling, which a relationship set, keyed only by its participants, could not record.

## **2.3 Relationships and Constraints**

| Relationship | Cardinality and participation | Reason |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Person IsA Student / Volunteer / Staff | Overlapping, total (covering) | One person can hold several roles (e.g. kevi5326 is a student and a volunteer); every registered person has at least one role. |
| Booking – Makes – Student | Booking 1..1 (thick arrow); Student 0..\* | Every booking belongs to one student; booking history is kept across days. |
| Booking – For – Session | Booking 1..1 (thick arrow); Session 0..\* | The upper bound of 50 is a business rule ER cannot express, so it is enforced in SQL (Section 4.3). |
| Booking – ApprovedBy – Staff | Booking 0..1 (thin arrow); Staff 0..\* | Only exception bookings name the staff member who approved them. |
| Session – BelongsTo – Shift | Session 1..1 (thick arrow); Shift 0..\* | A session cannot exist outside a shift; policy creates four per shift. |
| Staff – AssignedTo – Shift (attribute assignment\_role) | Shift 2..2 (thick line); Staff 0..\* | Every shift needs exactly two staff; the duty role belongs to the assignment, not the person. |
| ShiftRequest – Submits – Volunteer; ShiftRequest – ForShift – Shift (identifying relationships) | ShiftRequest 1..1 in both (thick arrow); Volunteer 0..\*, Shift 0..\* | An application only exists for one volunteer and one shift, and is identified by them. |
| ShiftRequest – Reviews – Staff | ShiftRequest 0..1 (thin arrow); Staff 0..\* | Staff approve or reject a specific application; pending ones have no reviewer yet. |
| PurchaseRecord – Records – Staff | PurchaseRecord 1..1 (thick arrow); Staff 0..\* | Every purchase is recorded by one staff member. |
| PurchaseLine – Contains – PurchaseRecord | PurchaseLine 1..1; PurchaseRecord 1..\* (thick line) | Invoice header/line structure; a record has at least one line. |
| PurchaseLine – Of – Product | PurchaseLine 1..1; Product 0..\* | Each line buys one product. |
| StockBatch – Supplies – PurchaseLine | StockBatch 1..1; PurchaseLine 0..\* | Every batch traces to the purchase that supplied it (BR8). |
| StockCount – CountOf – StockBatch; StockCount – CountedBy – Staff | StockCount 1..1 in both | Each count is of one batch and by one staff member. |
| StockCount – DuringShift – Shift | StockCount 0..1 (thin arrow); Shift 0..\* | Spot checks may happen outside a shift. |
| Shift – ShiftStock – StockBatch (attributes opening\_qty, closing\_qty, opening\_variance\_reason; multivalued adjustment {adjustment\_kind, quantity, reason}) | M:N, both 0..\* | Shift handover balance for each batch, with receipts and waste recorded during the shift. |

## **2.4 Design Rationale and Assumptions**

* **IsA instead of a role attribute.** Role-specific attributes (degree level, staff code) and role-specific relationships (only staff can be assigned to shifts) belong on subclasses. Overlap is allowed because student volunteers are common at FoodHub.  
* **Separate Shift and Session.** Staffing happens per 2-hour shift and booking per 30-minute session. Merging them would either repeat staffing four times or lose booking granularity.  
* **ShiftRequest as a weak entity.** A volunteer's application for a shift has its own state and is reviewed by a staff member, so it needs to take part in a relationship of its own. A plain M:N relationship cannot, and a ternary Staff–Volunteer–Shift relationship would wrongly allow a review without an application. Making the application a weak entity owned by Volunteer and Shift lets Reviews attach to it directly, and the thin arrow says each application is reviewed at most once.  
* **Product is reached through PurchaseLine.** A batch's product is not drawn as a separate relationship because it is already determined by the purchase line that supplied it. The logical design later copies product\_id into stock\_batch for performance; Section 3.4 treats this as a deliberate, controlled redundancy.  
* **Stock counts as events.** Each count is a StockCount entity rather than a "current quantity" attribute on StockBatch, which keeps the audit trail required by BR9; stock on hand is derived from the latest count.  
* **Adjustments as a multivalued attribute.** Within one shift a batch can have a receipt and a waste entry, each with its own quantity and reason, so adjustment is a multivalued composite attribute of ShiftStock rather than two fixed columns.  
* **Assumptions:** shift times and capacities are fixed by policy (10:00–16:00 operating day); dispensed quantities are estimated from counts rather than recorded per student, which protects student privacy.

Traceability to Section 1: BR1 → Person/IsA; BR2 → BelongsTo; BR3–BR6 → Booking, For, Makes, ApprovedBy; BR7 → AssignedTo, ShiftRequest, Reviews; BR8 → Supplies; BR9 → StockCount and ShiftStock. The rules listed under the diagram cannot be drawn and are enforced in SQL (Section 4.3).

# **3\. Logical Design and Normalisation**

## **3.1 Relational Schema**

Figure 2 is generated directly from the implemented PostgreSQL catalogue. Primary keys are underlined, (FK) marks foreign keys and arrows point to the referenced table, and (UQ) marks attributes that form a candidate (UNIQUE) key.

![][image2]

**Figure 2\. Relational (RM) diagram of the implemented schema (16 relations).**

| Relation | Primary key | Candidate keys | Foreign keys |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| person | unikey | – | – |
| student / volunteer / staff | unikey | staff: staff\_code | unikey → person |
| pantry\_shift | shift\_id | (shift\_date, start\_time) | – |
| session | session\_id | (session\_date, start\_time) | shift\_id → pantry\_shift (NOT NULL) |
| shift\_staff\_assignment | (shift\_id, staff\_unikey) | (shift\_id, assignment\_role) | shift\_id → pantry\_shift; staff\_unikey → staff |
| volunteer\_shift | (shift\_id, volunteer\_unikey) | – | → pantry\_shift, volunteer; reviewed\_by\_staff → staff |
| booking | booking\_id | qr\_token | student\_unikey → student; session\_id → session; override\_by\_staff → staff |
| product | product\_id | product\_code | – |
| purchase\_record | purchase\_id | – | recorded\_by\_staff → staff |
| purchase\_record\_line | purchase\_line\_id | – | purchase\_id → purchase\_record; product\_id → product |
| stock\_batch | stock\_number | – | product\_id → product; purchase\_line\_id → purchase\_record\_line |
| stock\_count | stock\_count\_id | – | stock\_number → stock\_batch; shift\_id → pantry\_shift; counted\_by\_staff → staff |
| shift\_stock\_count | (shift\_id, stock\_number) | – | → pantry\_shift, stock\_batch |
| stock\_adjustment | (shift\_id, stock\_number, adjustment\_kind) | – | (shift\_id, stock\_number) → shift\_stock\_count |

## **3.2 Mapping from ER Model to Relations**

* **IsA hierarchy.** Mapped with one relation per class (the "ER style" option). Each subclass table uses unikey as both primary key and foreign key to person. Because the hierarchy is overlapping, a single table with a type column would not work, and a table per subclass only (no person) would repeat name and email for people with several roles.  
* **1:N with key constraint and total participation.** BelongsTo, Makes, For, Records, Contains, Of, Supplies, CountOf and CountedBy are folded into the entity on the arrow side as NOT NULL foreign keys (e.g. session.shift\_id NOT NULL), which enforces both the key constraint and total participation.  
* **1:N without total participation.** ApprovedBy becomes the nullable column booking.override\_by\_staff, and DuringShift becomes the nullable stock\_count.shift\_id.  
* **M:N with attributes.** AssignedTo becomes shift\_staff\_assignment with PK (shift\_id, staff\_unikey) and the extra candidate key (shift\_id, assignment\_role), which gives "at most one supervisor and one assistant per shift" for free. ShiftStock becomes shift\_stock\_count.  
* **Weak entity.** ShiftRequest becomes volunteer\_shift, whose primary key is the owners' keys (shift\_id, volunteer\_unikey), each also a foreign key; the identifying relationships Submits and ForShift need no tables of their own. Because each request is reviewed at most once (key constraint), Reviews is folded in as the nullable foreign key reviewed\_by\_staff.  
* **Multivalued composite attribute.** adjustment becomes its own relation stock\_adjustment, keyed by the owner's key plus the distinguishing component: (shift\_id, stock\_number, adjustment\_kind), with a composite foreign key to shift\_stock\_count.  
* **Added at the logical level.** stock\_batch.product\_id is not in the ER model (it is implied by Supplies and Of); it was added on purpose and is analysed in 3.4.  
* **Derived values are not stored.** Spaces remaining, attendance rates and estimated dispensed quantities are computed in views (v\_booking\_attendance, v\_shift\_stock\_report), so they can never disagree with the base data.

## **3.3 Functional Dependencies**

FDs were derived from the business rules, not from sample data. The non-trivial ones that matter for normalisation are:

| Relation | Functional dependencies |
| :---- | :---- |
| staff | unikey → staff\_code, is\_active;  staff\_code → unikey |
| pantry\_shift | shift\_id → shift\_date, start\_time, end\_time, status;  {shift\_date, start\_time} → shift\_id |
| session | session\_id → all;  {session\_date, start\_time} → session\_id;  **shift\_id → session\_date** (a session lies on its shift's date, BR2) |
| shift\_staff\_assignment | {shift\_id, staff\_unikey} → assignment\_role;  {shift\_id, assignment\_role} → staff\_unikey |
| volunteer\_shift | {shift\_id, volunteer\_unikey} → status, request\_date, reviewed\_by\_staff, reviewed\_at |
| booking | booking\_id → all;  qr\_token → booking\_id |
| product | product\_id → all;  product\_code → product\_id |
| purchase\_record\_line | purchase\_line\_id → purchase\_id, product\_id, quantity, unit\_cost |
| stock\_batch | stock\_number → all;  **purchase\_line\_id → product\_id** (a batch is of the product that was purchased) |
| stock\_count | stock\_count\_id → stock\_number, shift\_id, counted\_by\_staff, counted\_at, count\_type, counted\_qty, notes |
| shift\_stock\_count | {shift\_id, stock\_number} → opening\_qty, closing\_qty, opening\_variance\_reason |
| stock\_adjustment | {shift\_id, stock\_number, adjustment\_kind} → quantity, reason |

Dependencies that look plausible but were deliberately *not* assumed: email → unikey (shared or changed emails are possible), and start\_time → end\_time in pantry\_shift (shift length is policy, not a law of the data).

## **3.4 Normalisation Analysis**

All relations are in 1NF (atomic attributes; multi-valued roles were split into subclass tables). For a relation R to be in BCNF, every non-trivial FD X → Y over R must have a superkey X (Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, 2003).

**Relations in BCNF (14 of 16).** In person, the three subclass tables, pantry\_shift, shift\_staff\_assignment, volunteer\_shift, booking, product, purchase\_record, purchase\_record\_line, stock\_count, shift\_stock\_count and stock\_adjustment, the left-hand side of every FD listed above is a candidate key, so they are in BCNF without decomposition. Two cases with more than one key are worth noting: in shift\_staff\_assignment both {shift\_id, staff\_unikey} and {shift\_id, assignment\_role} are candidate keys, so the FD between them does not break BCNF; in staff, staff\_code → unikey has a key on its left side.

**session: 3NF but not BCNF.** The FD shift\_id → session\_date has a left-hand side that is not a superkey (a shift has four sessions). It does not break 3NF, because session\_date is a prime attribute: it belongs to the candidate key {session\_date, start\_time}. The BCNF decomposition would be R1(shift\_id, session\_date) – which duplicates pantry\_shift(shift\_id, shift\_date) – and R2(session\_id, shift\_id, start\_time, end\_time, capacity). That decomposition is lossless, but it is **not dependency-preserving**: the key {session\_date, start\_time} → session\_id spans R1 and R2, so "no two sessions at the same date and time" could no longer be enforced by a UNIQUE constraint. Following the usual guidance to prefer 3NF when BCNF would lose a dependency (Silberschatz et al., 2020), we accept 3NF here, so the key stays declarative. The redundancy is controlled by trigger validate\_session\_shift(), which rejects any session whose date or times do not fit its shift (failure test 5).

**stock\_batch: deliberate 3NF violation.** stock\_number → purchase\_line\_id → product\_id is a transitive dependency on a non-prime attribute, so storing product\_id breaks 3NF. The normalised alternative is to drop product\_id and join through purchase\_record\_line. We kept product\_id because the most frequent operations (latest stock per product, low-stock and expiry reports) group batches by product, and the column lets the stock\_batch\_by\_product index serve them directly. The resulting update anomaly (a batch pointing to rice while its purchase line says pasta) is blocked by trigger validate\_stock\_batch\_product() on insert and update (failure test 8).

## **3.5 Final Design Decisions and Trade-offs**

* **Count history vs shift summary.** stock\_count is the authoritative, append-only event log; the ShiftStock quantities in shift\_stock\_count.closing\_qty repeat the closing count so the handover report and Q6 variance query are simple. The duplication is controlled by writing both in a single transaction (Transaction E, Section 4.4), and validation check 8 verifies the stock arithmetic.  
* **One adjustment row per kind per shift.** The key (shift\_id, stock\_number, adjustment\_kind) keeps the report join one-to-one; the prototype adds repeated receipts to the existing quantity. The cost is that only the latest reason text is kept, which we accepted for a shift-level report.  
* **Surrogate keys.** Identity columns are used for shifts, sessions and bookings so that foreign keys stay short and stable, but the natural keys ((date, start\_time), qr\_token, product\_code, staff\_code) are still declared UNIQUE so duplicates are impossible.  
* **Rules that cannot be keys.** Capacity, one-booking-per-day, staffing completeness and overlap rules involve counts across rows, so they are triggers rather than CHECK constraints (Section 4.3).  
* **Known limitation.** validate\_session\_shift() fires on changes to session, not to pantry\_shift. Changing a shift's date after its sessions exist would leave them inconsistent, so shift times are treated as fixed once sessions are generated.

# **4\. SQL, Integrity and Transactions**

## **4.1 PostgreSQL Implementation**

The database lives in schema campus\_pantry on PostgreSQL 16 and is rebuilt from the submitted scripts in this order:

| File | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- |
| 01\_schema.sql | 16 tables, CHECK/UNIQUE/FK constraints, 6 indexes, 6 trigger functions, 3 views |
| 02\_seed\_data.sql | Synthetic data for one operating day (9 Oct 2026\) and resets identity sequences |
| 03\_queries.sql | 12 management queries (Q1–Q12) |
| 04\_transactions.sql | Transaction scenarios A–F |
| 05\_validation.sql | 12 integrity checks that should return no violations |
| 06\_failure\_tests.sql | 10 negative/boundary tests in PL/pgSQL (each cleans up after itself) |
| campus\_pantry\_app/test\_all\_rules.py | 17 end-to-end tests through the Python service layer, including a concurrency race |

The seed data contains 29 people (17 students, 9 volunteers, 4 staff, with one student who is also a volunteer), 3 closed shifts with 12 sessions, 6 staff assignments, 10 volunteer registrations, 15 bookings, 1 purchase with 8 lines, 8 products and batches, 48 stock-count events, 24 shift stock rows and 5 adjustments. A one-shot script, campus\_pantry\_app/sql/rebuild\_campus\_pantry.sql, drops and recreates everything; we checked that it produces the same schema as running 01 and 02 separately.

## **4.2 Representative SQL Operations**

The table summarises the 12 queries and the result each gives on the seed data. Two are shown in full below.

| Query | Requirement served | Techniques | Result on seed data |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Q1 | Shift stock movement report | View with two LEFT JOINs to the same table, CASE, COALESCE | 24 rows (8 batches × 3 shifts) |
| Q2 | Total dispensed per product | Aggregation over view, GROUP BY, ORDER BY | Rice 57, oat milk 35, bread 28 … |
| Q3 | Latest count per batch | DISTINCT ON with ORDER BY counted\_at DESC | 8 rows, all CLOSING counts |
| Q4 | Products below reorder threshold | CTEs, DISTINCT ON, LEFT JOIN, SUM | 0 rows (all above threshold) |
| Q5 | Places left per session | View with COUNT … FILTER | 12 sessions; sessions 1–2 hold 7 and 8 bookings |
| Q6 | Handover variance between shifts | LATERAL subquery with LIMIT 1 | 1 row: rice \+2 at shift 2 with reason |
| Q7 | Products never dispensed | Correlated NOT EXISTS | 0 rows |
| Q8 | Staff and volunteer roster | Multi-table joins, filter APPROVED | 6 staff duties, 10 volunteers |
| Q9 | Purchase cost by product | Three-table join, SUM(qty × cost) | 560 units, \$1,050 total |
| Q10 | Attendance rate per session | FILTER, NULLIF to avoid ÷0, ROUND | Rate per session (NULL when no bookings) |
| Q11 | Batches expiring in 30 days | Date arithmetic with CURRENT\_DATE | 0 rows on 24 Oct 2026; the bread and apple batches had already expired (15 and 20 Oct), and this range does not include expired stock |
| Q12 | Sessions ≥ 80% full | View \+ CEIL(capacity × 0.8) | 0 rows on seed; flagged in tests |

**Q6 – handover variance.** For each shift's opening count, the LATERAL subquery finds the closing count of the most recent earlier closed shift for the same batch. The end\_time \<= start\_time condition links back-to-back shifts on the same day.

SELECT cur.shift\_id, cur.stock\_number, cur.opening\_qty,  
       prev.closing\_qty AS previous\_closing\_qty,  
       cur.opening\_qty \- prev.closing\_qty AS variance\_qty,  
       cur.opening\_variance\_reason  
FROM shift\_stock\_count cur  
JOIN pantry\_shift cur\_shift ON cur\_shift.shift\_id \= cur.shift\_id  
JOIN LATERAL (  
    SELECT s2.closing\_qty  
    FROM shift\_stock\_count s2  
    JOIN pantry\_shift sh2 ON sh2.shift\_id \= s2.shift\_id  
    WHERE s2.stock\_number \= cur.stock\_number AND sh2.status \= 'CLOSED'  
      AND (sh2.shift\_date \< cur\_shift.shift\_date  
           OR (sh2.shift\_date \= cur\_shift.shift\_date  
               AND sh2.end\_time \<= cur\_shift.start\_time))  
    ORDER BY sh2.shift\_date DESC, sh2.end\_time DESC  
    LIMIT 1\) prev ON true  
WHERE cur.opening\_qty \- prev.closing\_qty \<\> 0;

 shift\_id \| stock\_number \| opening\_qty \| previous\_closing\_qty \| variance\_qty  
        2 \| STK-000001   \|          92 \|                   90 \|            2  
 opening\_variance\_reason: Found 2 misplaced packs on shelf during handover

**Q4 – low stock.** Stock on hand is not stored. It is the sum of the latest count of each batch, found with DISTINCT ON, compared with the product's threshold. Products with no counts still appear (LEFT JOIN with COALESCE to 0).

WITH batch\_latest AS (  
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (sc.stock\_number) sc.stock\_number, sb.product\_id, sc.counted\_qty  
    FROM stock\_count sc JOIN stock\_batch sb USING (stock\_number)  
    ORDER BY sc.stock\_number, sc.counted\_at DESC, sc.stock\_count\_id DESC),  
product\_totals AS (  
    SELECT p.product\_id, p.product\_name, p.low\_stock\_threshold,  
           COALESCE(SUM(bl.counted\_qty), 0\) AS last\_known\_quantity  
    FROM product p LEFT JOIN batch\_latest bl ON bl.product\_id \= p.product\_id  
    GROUP BY p.product\_id)  
SELECT \* FROM product\_totals  
WHERE last\_known\_quantity \< low\_stock\_threshold;

Data modification statements are covered in Section 4.4 (INSERT booking, UPDATE check-in and cancellation, UPDATE … FROM for no-shows, INSERT \+ UPDATE for stock counts).

## **4.3 Integrity Constraints**

| Type | Mechanism (01\_schema.sql) | Rule |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Key | PRIMARY KEY on all 16 tables; UNIQUE on qr\_token, staff\_code, product\_code, (shift\_date, start\_time), (session\_date, start\_time), (shift\_id, assignment\_role) | BR1, BR2, BR5, BR7 |
| Domain | CHECK on UniKey regex ^\[a-z\]{4}\[0-9\]{4}\$; status enumerations; capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 50; counted\_qty ≥ 0; quantity \> 0; end\_time \> start\_time; expires\_on ≥ received\_on | BR1, BR3, BR9 |
| Referential | 23 FOREIGN KEYs, NOT NULL where participation is total (e.g. session.shift\_id) | BR2, BR8 |
| Tuple-level | CHECK (status \<\> 'ATTENDED' OR attendance\_at IS NOT NULL); CHECK admin\_override ⇔ override\_by\_staff present | BR4, BR5 |
| Cross-row (triggers) | validate\_booking() – capacity and one booking per day, with row locks; validate\_shift\_status() – exactly 1 supervisor \+ 1 assistant before OPEN/CLOSED; validate\_staff\_shift\_overlap(), validate\_volunteer\_shift\_overlap(); validate\_session\_shift(); validate\_stock\_batch\_product() | BR2–BR4, BR7, BR8 |

Examples of invalid operations being rejected (output of 06\_failure\_tests.sql):

\[PASS\] Test 1: Duplicate daily booking was rejected.  
        (Student already has an active booking on this date)  
\[PASS\] Test 2: Admin override without staff was rejected.  
        (Admin override must identify the staff member)  
\[PASS\] Test 3: Session capacity boundary (50 accepted, 51st rejected) strictly enforced.  
\[PASS\] Test 4: Invalid UniKey format was rejected.  
        (new row for relation "person" violates check constraint "person\_unikey\_check")

\[PASS\] Test 8: Mismatched stock batch product was rejected.

Rules are enforced in the database, not only in Python, so they also hold for anyone using psql or pgAdmin directly. The Python layer repeats some checks only to give friendlier messages.

## **4.4 Transaction Scenario**

**Main scenario: booking a session** (services.book\_session, also scenario A in 04\_transactions.sql). It is one transaction because a booking is only valid if all of these steps see the same state:

BEGIN;  \-- opened by psycopg2; \`with conn:\` commits, or rolls back on error  
\-- 1\. lock the student row  
SELECT unikey FROM student WHERE unikey \= %s FOR UPDATE;  
\-- 2\. session exists and has not finished  
SELECT (session\_date \+ end\_time) \< localtimestamp, session\_date  
FROM session WHERE session\_id \= %s;  
\-- 3\. insert; BEFORE INSERT trigger validate\_booking() then:  
\--    SELECT ... FROM session WHERE session\_id \= NEW.session\_id FOR UPDATE;  
\--    count active bookings in the session  \-\> RAISE if \>= capacity  
\--    count student's active bookings that day \-\> RAISE unless override  
INSERT INTO booking (student\_unikey, session\_id, qr\_token, admin\_override,  
                     override\_by\_staff, override\_reason)  
VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s) RETURNING booking\_id;  
COMMIT;  \-- QR token is shown to the student only after commit

The boundary is from the eligibility check to the insert. If the checks and the insert ran as separate transactions, another booking could commit in between and the check would be stale.

**Other transactions** in 04\_transactions.sql: (B) QR check-in – a single conditional UPDATE … WHERE qr\_token \= ? AND status \= 'CONFIRMED', so a second scan changes 0 rows; (C) cancellation, which frees the place at once because capacity counts only non-cancelled rows; (D) end-of-day no-shows using UPDATE … FROM session after 16:00; (E) closing stock count – INSERT into stock\_count **and** UPDATE shift\_stock\_count.closing\_qty, which must commit together or the audit log and the handover report would disagree; (F) an explicit ROLLBACK showing nothing persists.

## **4.5 Failure and Concurrency Reasoning**

**Failure and rollback (atomicity).** Every write in the prototype runs inside with conn:. Any exception – a trigger's RAISE, a CHECK violation or a Python error – rolls back the whole transaction. In Transaction E, if the UPDATE of shift\_stock\_count fails (e.g. a negative quantity), the already-executed INSERT into stock\_count is also undone, so no half-recorded count remains. Test 14 of test\_all\_rules.py shows this: the booking count is identical before and after an aborted transaction.

**The concurrency problem.** PostgreSQL's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL Global Development Group, n.d.). Without locks, two transactions can both count 49 bookings in a 50-place session, both pass the check and both insert, so the session ends up with 51\. The same pattern lets one student get two bookings on the same day from two devices. This is a lost-update style anomaly: the interleaved schedule is not conflict-serializable, because each transaction's read is overwritten by the other's write.

**Solution: row-level locks held to commit.** validate\_booking() takes an exclusive lock on the session row and on the student row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) before counting. PostgreSQL holds these locks until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, as in strict two-phase locking (Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, 2003), so a second transaction for the same session or student waits. When it resumes, READ COMMITTED gives the trigger's next statement a fresh snapshot, so it sees the committed booking and correctly raises the capacity or duplicate error. Transactions for different sessions and students do not block each other, so concurrency is kept where it is safe. The locks are taken inside the trigger, so the rule holds even for SQL that bypasses the prototype.

**Evidence.** Test 11 starts two threads racing for the last place in a session. Exactly one wins and the other gets "Session capacity … has been reached"; the final count equals capacity. concurrency\_demo.py has the same student book two sessions at once; the second request waits for the first to commit and is then rejected.

**Deadlock.** The service layer locks the student and then the session; the trigger locks the session and then the student (the student lock is already held, so it is a no-op). A transaction from the prototype and a hand-written INSERT for the same student and session could therefore wait on each other. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, which is rolled back and reported as an error, so data stays correct. Using a single lock order everywhere would remove this case.
